title: Hamlin citrus: Fruit and Tree Characteristics
metaTitle: Hamlin citrus: Fruit and Tree Characteristics
metaDescription: Hamlin citrus is a sweet orange citrus variety from BPI Baguio NCRDC. See its days to harvest, yield, pest ratings, traits and where it grows best.
excerpt: Hamlin citrus is a sweet orange citrus variety, also sold or known as Hamlin (sweet orange) or Hamlin orange. It was registered with the National Seed Industry Council in 2005 as NSIC 2005 On 01. BPI Baguio NCRDC, Baguio City bred it.

blocks.text: If you came here looking for Hamlin (sweet orange) or Hamlin orange, this is the same citrus. Its seller and farm sources add notes, listed at the end. Compare it with the others in our [citrus variety finder](/crop-varieties/citrus), or see [every crop variety](/crop-varieties) we list. For the crop itself, read our guide: [fertilizer for fruit trees](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).

blocks.caption: Key facts of Hamlin
rows: Hamlin (sweet orange), Hamlin orange, NSIC On 01

blocks.text: When does it bear, and how much?

A registered tree variety is described from its mother tree, not from trial plots. The mother tree of Hamlin was about 8 years old and about 2.5 meters tall when it was registered. It bears every year, with fruit in March September. Each tree gave about 60 kilograms in the records. A grafted or marcotted tree bears years sooner than one grown from seed, and its yield climbs as the tree grows.

anee.io keeps the records of each block of trees, from fertilizer to harvest, with [the growth stages and weather](/features/growth-stages-and-weather) beside them.
Is it resistant to pests and diseases?
No pest or disease ratings are published for this variety. So treat it as untested, and scout every week.

The pests and diseases that hit citrus fields most often: [citrus greening](/diseases/citrus-greening), [mealybug](/pests/mealybug), [Oriental fruit fly](/pests/oriental-fruit-fly). Our [pest finder](/pests) and [disease finder](/diseases) help you name what you see.

A fruit of Hamlin weighs about 200 grams, and its shape is spheroid. The flesh is yellow and soft. Its sweetness measured 12.33 degrees Brix, the share of sugar in the juice. Most table fruit tastes sweet from about 12 Brix up. The edible part is 81.42 percent of the fruit. Its fruiting season is March September, bearing annual.
What its seller and farm sources say

items: **Fruit:** Round, about 200 g, yellow peel, juicy yellow flesh, about 12.3 Brix, low acidity.

blocks.text: Why farmers know it: a vigorous, low acid sweet orange registered by BPI Baguio, about 60 kg per tree. Check these against what farmers near you have seen, because the same variety can do differently from one town to the next.
Where and when to plant Hamlin citrus

Sweet oranges and mandarins grow best in the cooler, drier parts of the country. Buy budded trees on a tested rootstock from an accredited nursery, and keep out greening disease. A registered tree variety is a selection from one proven mother tree, and only grafted, budded or marcotted plants carry its traits. A seedling grown from its seed can turn out quite different. So buy from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, and ask which mother tree the scions came from. Before planting, get the field ready with our guide: [Land preparation for fruit trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation).

items: Buy grafted or budded plants from an accredited nursery, with the variety name on the tag.
Ask your municipal agriculturist or nearby farmers how it did in your area last season.
Plant a few trees first if the variety is new to your area, before you fill the whole farm.
Write down the planting day, inputs and harvest, so you can compare varieties on your own ground. anee.io keeps these records for you.

items.q: Is Hamlin (sweet orange) the same as Hamlin?
items.a: Yes. Hamlin (sweet orange) is another name for Hamlin, registered as NSIC 2005 On 01. Seed sellers use both, so ask for either one.

items.q: Where can I buy planting material of Hamlin?
items.a: Buy grafted, budded or marcotted trees from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, so you get the true variety. Ask your provincial agriculture office for the nearest one.
